messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 48

He is 67 and still introduces himself the way he always has: as a school principal, a man used to keeping things orderly, predictable, and under control. For most of his adult life, that identity has fit him well. He is a European man, married for many years, with a steady manner and a habit of speaking carefully, as if each word should be useful. Before the crash, he describes himself as someone who trusted routine, who left home at the same time each morning, took the same route to school, and believed that if he stayed organized enough, most problems could be handled.

The collision changes that sense of safety in an instant. He is driving on an ordinary day when another vehicle comes fast and wrong, and there is no time to react. He remembers the force of impact, the violent sound of metal, the sudden loss of control. In the sessions, he returns often to the moment just after the crash, the strange silence that follows the noise, the feeling that he cannot quite understand whether he is alive until he notices pain, blood, and the wrecked interior of the car. He says that for a few seconds he is certain he is dying. That belief stays with him long after the physical danger passes.

In the days after, he is shaken by how much his body seems to know before his mind does. He wakes in the night with his heart racing, already braced for impact. At times he feels the crash before he even fully remembers it, a sharp tightening in his chest when he hears tires screech outside or when someone brakes too suddenly at an intersection. He begins avoiding driving when he can, and when he must go out, he chooses routes that feel slower and less exposed, even if they take longer. He is embarrassed by how much effort this takes, because he has spent his life being the one who others rely on. At school, he notices that he is more irritable and less patient than usual. Noise in the hallways unsettles him. The slam of a door can leave him disoriented for several seconds. He finds himself scanning the parking lot before he enters his car, then checking the mirrors again and again, as if vigilance might prevent a repetition of what happened.

Over time, he notices that memory itself becomes unreliable. Certain details come back with an almost physical force: the angle of the other car, the smell of gasoline, the sound of his own breathing as he tried to remain conscious. Other parts feel oddly distant, as if they belong to someone else’s story. He becomes frustrated with himself when he loses track of what he is saying mid-sentence or when he stands in his office and cannot remember why he walked into the room. He is not confused in a broader way, but he feels less anchored, as though part of his attention is always remaining at the site of the accident. His wife tells him he is withdrawn, and he knows she is right. At home, he sits through dinner more quietly than before. He still performs the practical parts of married life, but with less ease and less humor. He does not want to burden her, so he minimizes how bad it feels.

He also carries a private shame about vulnerability. As principal, he is accustomed to being decisive, to responding calmly when students are frightened or when staff need direction. After the crash, he starts to feel less like the steady center of things and more like someone holding himself together through effort alone. He worries about appearing weak. This makes him hide the extent of his distress, though his body gives him away. His sleep remains disrupted, and he drifts through mornings feeling as if he has not fully rested. He avoids the news when there are reports of serious accidents. He dislikes being a passenger because he cannot control the speed or the distance between cars. In heavy traffic, his muscles tense before he notices they are tense.

Even now, months later, the collision is never entirely past. It lives in the way he pauses at intersections, in the flash of alarm that moves through him when he hears sudden metal-on-metal sounds, in the way his chest tightens before he can explain why. He still goes to work, still leads meetings, still greets students with the measured warmth that has made him effective for so long. But he experiences the day with a background current of danger that others do not see. He describes himself as functioning, but not at ease, as if part of him is always listening for the next collision.
